title: This ‘Spider-Man’ Art Book Explores the Making of ‘Brand New Day,’ From Early Concept Sketches to Final Production Designs
description:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Spider-Ma
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Spider-Man is swinging from the big screen to the coffee table.

	A new hardcover book exploring the making of Tom Holland’s latest Marvel adventure  is now available to pre-order on Amazon ahead of its Aug. 18 release. The 208-page book, written by Jess Harrold, takes readers behind the scenes of the superhero sequel’s visual development, from early concept sketches to the final character, costume and production designs seen onscreen. 


	The book should also offer a closer look at Spider-Man’s redesigned suit, which marks a return to the hero’s more traditional comic-book appearance. The costume pairs brighter red-and-blue coloring with prominent raised webbing and a larger black spider emblem across the chest, moving away from the sleek, Stark-designed technology that defined many of Holland’s earlier suits.

	The release arrives as “Brand New Day” continues its record-breaking theatrical run. The Sony Pictures and Marvel Studios film opened to $360 million in North America, surpassing “Avengers: Endgame” for the biggest domestic opening weekend of all time. Globally, it launched with approximately $932 million, the second-largest worldwide opening in history behind “Endgame.”

	Directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, the fourth standalone Spider-Man film starring Holland picks up after the events of 2021’s “Spider-Man: No Way Home,” which ended with the world forgetting Peter Parker’s identity. Now living alone and fighting crime full time, Peter finds himself facing a mysterious new threat while watching his former friends move forward without him.


	Zendaya and Jacob Batalon return as MJ and Ned, respectively, while the ensemble also includes Sadie Sink, Jon Bernthal, Tramell Tillman, Michael Mando and Mark Ruffalo.

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day — The Art of the Movie” is available to pre-order on Amazon for $46.60 and will be released Aug. 18.

title: ‘Miss Navajo’ Musical in the Works From Director Billy Luther and Singer-Songwriter Raye Zaragoza (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
“Frybread Face and Me” director Billy Luther is adapting his 2007 documentary “Miss Navajo” into a musical, which is currently in development.

	Now
body:
“Frybread Face and Me” director Billy Luther is adapting his 2007 documentary “Miss Navajo” into a musical, which is currently in development.

	Now, 19 years after the world premiere at 2007’s Sundance Film Festival, Luther has teamed up with singer-songwriter Raye Zaragoza to bring the documentary to the stage.

	Luther said, “I am thrilled to be working with Raye to bring ‘Miss Navajo’ to the stage.” He added, “Raye’s thought provoking strength of Indigenous women resonates.” He adds, “I was raised by Navajo women. My mother eventually was crowned in 1966. Her culture, traditions and language remained, and this is the resiliency I see in Indigenous women every day.”
	

	“I am so excited to be collaborating with Billy on the theater vision of Miss Navajo and go on this musical journey together. He’s such a visionary and we both speak a similar language with music,” said Zaragoza.


	The documentary film follows Crystal Frazier, a 21-year-old woman from near Table Mesa, New Mexico, who initially doubts her ability to succeed in the Miss Navajo Nation pageant and is uncertain whether she belongs among the other contestants. The film follows the five-day competition at the Navajo Nation Fair, where seven contestants are evaluated in a series of events designed to test their knowledge of Navajo culture and language.

	Luther’s (Dine, Hopi, Laguna Pueblo) own mother was crowned Miss Navajo 1966. The film reveals the inner beauty of the young women who compete in this celebration of womanhood. Not only must contestants exhibit poise and grace as those in typical pageants, but they must also answer tough questions in Navajo and demonstrate proficiency in skills essential to daily tribal life: frybread making, rug weaving and sheep butchering.
	

	Zaragoza (Akimel O’otham descent) will pull from her career catalog and new work for Miss Navajo, with songs and lyrics about Indigenous women, cultural strength, immigration and the environment.

	Miss Navajo is not your typical beauty pageant. Anyone can sign up to participate, provided they are female, single and older than 18, but they must be prepared to shear, butcher and cook a sheep over a fire outdoors. They must be well versed in Navajo legends. They must have an idea of what they would like to teach all 250,000 residents of the reservation. Above all, the recent high school graduates must be able to speak and understand the Navajo, or Dine, language.

	At the time of the film’s release, about Luther said, “What inspired me about the beauty pageant was that here was a crossroads where the Western competition met Native influences, and the result was something not gaudy and glitzy like most beauty pageants, but something beautiful and profound, something that really reveals the true essence of beauty and in so doing, I think, provides a compelling insight into what it is that both makes my culture and heritage unique but also relevant to today’s world.”

title: David Z, Longtime Prince Associate and Key Architect of ‘the Minneapolis Sound,’ Dies at 78
description: David “Z” Rivkin, the Grammy-winning producer and musician who helmed Prince’s early demo tapes and engineered several of his albums, helped create
body:
David “Z” Rivkin, the Grammy-winning producer and musician who helmed Prince’s early demo tapes and engineered several of his albums, helped create Lipps Inc.’s 1980 smash “Funky Town,” and later worked with such artists like Fine Young Cannibals, the Jets and Jonny Lang, has died, his brother Bobby “Z” Rivkin (longtime drummer for Prince & the Revolution) confirmed to the Minnesota Star Tribune.

	He died Sunday from complications of an infection in a hospital in Burbank, Calif., his brother said; he was 78.
	

	Rivkin won two Grammys for producing Etta James and a nomination for co-producing Fine Young Cannibals’ 1989 smash “She Drives Me Crazy.”

	As a producer, engineer, songwriter and guitarist, Rivkin was an active and veteran member of the Minneapolis scene that spawned Prince, Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis and other future members of the Revolution and the Time, among many others. 

	“David was the secret ingredient on many, many musical projects,” Owen Husney, Rivkin’s former bandmate and Prince’s first manager, told the Star Tribune. “He stayed pretty silent about it. He never really talked about his work or what he did. His significance is undeniable on the Minneapolis music scene.”

	Over the years he also worked with such artists as Gram Parsons, Elvis Costello, Al Green, Jody Watley, Angelique Kidjo, Big Head Todd & the Monsters and Buddy Guy.

	The eldest of three brothers (the middle brother, Stephen, is a film editor who has worked on the “Avatar” and “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchises), David Rivkin’s credits reach back to the 1960s, when he played guitar on the regional hits “Little Latin Lupe Lu” by the Chancellors and “Turn on Your Lovelight” by the High Spirits. He later worked in Los Angeles as a staff songwriter at A&M Records, writing songs with Parsons and playing guitar on records by Billy Preston and the Rev. James Cleveland.
	

	But in 1974, he returned to Minneapolis and learned engineering. Husney recalled introducing an 18-year-old Prince to Rivkin in 1976 and played his demos. After Rivkin made some suggestions, Husney recalled, “Prince turned to me and said: ‘Let’s go. Let’s get out of here.’ I was embarrassed. I told David, ‘I’m sorry.’ I got in the car and said, ‘What happened?’ Prince said: ‘David is the only one I want working with me.’”

	That demo led to Prince signing with Warner Bros. Records in 1977; he remained with the label for nearly 20 years. Rivkin worked on multiple Prince projects over the years, including the live recordings that formed the basis for three songs on the classic “Purple Rain” album and film.

	He is survived by his two brothers and children Charley, Amy, Josh and Shelby as well as two grandchildren.

title: ‘God of War’: Dave Bautista in Talks For Kratos Role in Amazon Series After Ryan Hurst’s Exit
description: Dave Bautista could be the next “God of War.” Variety has learned from sources that Bautista is currently in talks for the role of Kratos in the Ama
body:
Dave Bautista could be the next “God of War.” Variety has learned from sources that Bautista is currently in talks for the role of Kratos in the Amazon Prime Video series based on the popular video game franchise.

	The news comes after it was reported that Ryan Hurst, who was originally cast in the role of the titular god in January 2026, suffered a torn bicep on the set of the series that would have delayed a return to production until 2027, ultimately leading Amazon and Sony to recast the part. The plan is to get the production back up and running by the fall.
	

	Reps for Amazon declined to comment. 


	There are few better suited for the role of Kratos than Bautista. Aside from the fact he is an accomplished actor, he is one of few in Hollywood who could step into the role on short notice in the physical shape it requires. Kratos is known for his incredibly muscular physique in the games, and Bautista has been in remarkable shape throughout his career. Thus, he would not need months of prep time to prepare for the role.

	He also has an existing relationship with Amazon MGM Studios. He previously starred in the Amazon movies “The Wrecking Crew,” “My Spy,” and “My Spy: The Eternal City,” while he is set to appear in both “Road House 2” and the remake of “Highlander” for Amazon.

	Bautista first broke out as a star in WWE before he transitioned to a highly successful and diverse acting career. He has played Drax in the Marvel Cinematic Universe across six movies, while he also appeared in the first two “Dune” films from Denis Villeneuve. He also recently lent his voice to the animated film “Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender,” and has previously starred in films like “Blade Runner 2049,” “Knock at the Cabin,” “Spectre,” and “Army of the Dead.” 
	

	He is repped by WME and Jackoway Austen Tyerman. 

	Prime Video has given “God of War” a two-season order. As previously reported, the series will pick up with the story of the two most recent “God of War” games, in which Kratos must raise his ten-year old son Atreus while battling gods of the Norse pantheon. Per the logline, “Father and son Kratos and Atreus embark on a journey to spread the ashes of their wife and mother, Faye. Through their adventures, Kratos tries to teach his son to be a better god, while Atreus tries to teach his father how to be a better human.”

	Callum Vinson remains attached to play Kratos’ son Atreus. Additional cast members include Max Parker as Heimdall, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson as Thor, Mandy Patinkin as Odin, Alastair Duncan as Mimir, Danny Woodburn and Jeff Gulka as as brothers Brok and Sindri, and Ed Skrein as Baldur.

	Ronald D. Moore is the writer, executive producer, and showrunner on “God of War” under his Tall Ship Productions banner.

	Frederick E.O. Toye will direct the first two episodes of “God of War.” Maril Davis of Tall Ship also executive produces alongside Cory Barlog, Naren Shankar, Matthew Graham, Asad Qizilbash, Jeff Ketcham, Hermen Hulst, Roy Lee, and Brad Van Arragon. Joe Menosky, Marc Bernardin, Tania Lotia, and Ben McGinnis serve as co-executive producers on the series. The series is co-produced by Sony Pictures Television and Amazon MGM Studios in association with PlayStation Productions and Tall Ship Productions.

title: TKO Raises Investor Guidance Again as UFC and WWE Flex Muscle With Fans and Marketers
description:
TKO posted another strong quarter fueled by strong demand from fans and marketers for UFC and WWE events. 

	The parent company of the two leagues s
body:
TKO posted another strong quarter fueled by strong demand from fans and marketers for UFC and WWE events. 

	The parent company of the two leagues surpassed the Street’s expectations on revenue and adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization with its second quarter results released Monday. TKO raised its full-year revenue guidance by another $75 million while full-year adjusted EBITDA is projected to be up by $25 million.
	

	“Despite a challenging global environment, TKO delivered solid results in Q2, with strong momentumheading into the back half of the year,” said Ariel Emanuel, executive chair and CEO of TKO. “Premiumlive content and experiences are heating up in an increasingly AI-driven world, and our businesses arewell positioned to fully capitalize on societal secular tailwinds.”


	As of today, TKO is raising its guidance for full-year 2026 revenue of $5.775 billion to $5.825 billion and Adjusted EBITDA of $2.275 billion to $2.305 billion.

	“From UFC Freedom 250 to the FIFA World Cup, TKO continues to deliver on the biggest stages andthis quarter reinforced our 2026 execution story. Our decision to raise full-year guidance reflects both our performance to date and our confidence in TKO’s multi-year trajectory,” said Mark Shapiro, presidentand COO of TKO. “Our global fan base is expanding, and we are capitalizing on the commercial promiseacross ticketing, premium hospitality, marketing partnerships, and financial incentive packages. Thedemand in the experience economy is undeniable and positions us well for multi-year growth, marginexpansion and overall value creation.”
	

	For the quarter, TKO in total delivered revenue of $1.547 billion, up 18% from the year-ago quarter, with net income of $303.9 million and adjusted EBITDA of $649.9 million.

	More to come

title: Jimmy Fallon is Nearly Last Late-Night Host Standing Amid Summer Hiatus
description:
And then there was Fallon.

	NBC‘s “Tonight Show” is the only late-night program to keep on keeping on as usual as the nation moves into late summer
body:
And then there was Fallon.

	NBC‘s “Tonight Show” is the only late-night program to keep on keeping on as usual as the nation moves into late summer, a sign of how the wee-hours format continues to be winnowed down amid a continuing decline in the economics of midnight TV.

	NBC this week launched what is expected to be a seven-week hiatus for Seth Meyers’ “Late Night,” the longest break of its kind since the host took over the show in 2014, according to people familiar with the matter. The LateNighter web site previously reported the new interruption. Social feeds belonging to “Late Night” on Monday told followers “See you in the fall!” and offered a link to reserve tickets to see the program live. Comedy Central’s “Daily Show” has also gone on a summer hiatus, and will be off for five weeks before returning in September. The network will not show repeats, and will instead feature other programming.
	

	These moves leave Jimmy Fallon as the only regular late-night host continuing to show up to make new programming over the next few weeks. In some ways, the scene is a throwback to the days when Johnny Carson hosted the show before some media companies enlisted Arsenio Hall or Joan Rivers to try and knock him off his wee-hours throne.  Jimmy Kimmel is on summer vacation, and his ABC program has relied on guest hosts. Tonight, the show features a repeat of a previous guest’s stint. Stephen Colbert is in exile, and CBS is no longer competing in late night, though it has leased two hours in the time slot to entrepreneur Byron Allen.  


	Late-night TV is in something of a retrenchment mode, with the rise of streaming luring away viewers who in the past made sure to tune in to their favorite host holding forth after the end of the late local news.  Ad spending on late-night television shows fell to $209 million in 2025, according to data from Guideline, a tracker of ad spending, down from $519.7 million in 2017 — a drop-off of nearly 60%.
	

	And talent contracts for many late-night hosts are getting shorter. Kimmel recently signed a surprising one-year deal with Disney that will keep him on his after-hours roost though 2027. John Oliver just agreed to a one-year extension with Warner Bros. Discovery’s HBO. Jon Stewart’s deal to host and produce “The Daily Show” has been negotiated in one-year extensions since he returned to the program in 2024.

	Both Fallon and Meyers have longer-term guarantees — at least for now. Their deals won’t expire until 2028.

schema.headline: Jimmy Fallon is Nearly Last Late-Night Host Standing Amid Summer Hiatus

title: Why Parents Are Still Afraid of Video Games After 50 Years and How a Gaming Nonprofit’s New Workshops Are Trying to Help
description: It’s been nearly six decades since the first mainstream video games came out and parents in 2026 are just as worried about the potential impact gami
body:
It’s been nearly six decades since the first mainstream video games came out and parents in 2026 are just as worried about the potential impact gaming is having on their children today as their counterparts were in the 70s, according to new research from the nonprofit Games for Change.

	In her paper “Raising Good Gamers: What Families Need to Know About Video Games and Well-Being,” which was released in July by Games for Change, research director Rachel Kowert drew on analysis of nearly 200,000 media articles and social posts across 15 countries and seven languages to reveal on social media, negative sentiment about gaming outweighs positive sentiment by more than five to one (34% to 6%).
	

	Kowert’s work found parents’ biggest concerns — screen time, addiction, and violent or age-inappropriate content — are based on common assumptions that are misaligned with the research. 


	“What I find most interesting is that the concerns that parents have today in 2026 are the same concerns that parents have had for the last 50 years: overexposure to inappropriate content, overuse and overdependence,” Kowert tells Variety. “So the fact that they have the same concerns tells me as a researcher that we’ve done a very poor job at getting the information out that we have in the research community to parents about what we know about what games are and what they aren’t.”

	Kowert notes that while society has repeated the pattern of being afraid of the effects of new types of media and entertainment throughout the centuries (including books, films and TV), the fears about gaming have persisted for longer.
	

	“I do see it being specific to gaming for a few reasons,” Kowert says. “One is because nothing has overtaken it. We have concerns about social media, but gaming is kind of different. It is also interactive. The other thing about gaming is with the media ecosystem we see a terrible violent crime happening and immediately it gets tagged with, ‘Oh that person played video games.’ And we’ve seen that, again, for the last 50 years. So there is something unique about this conversation. And sometimes I get pushback where they say, ‘Oh, well, social media has come.’ OK, we also do have fears about social media, which we now see, but it hasn’t replaced gaming because those fears still persist.”

	Kowert’s research found that nearly 60% of children say they want to play more games with their parents and suggested a system called “SPACE” for parents who want to engage: “Show up with curiosity, Play together, Adjust for context, Cultivate digital citizenship, and Establish boundaries together.” 

	“It’s interestingly an argument for allowing gameplay at a younger age, so that you do start to build a foundation,” Games for Change chief program and operating officer Arana Shapiro says. “With the assumption that because so many kids are playing games, teens especially, that if you assume that your child is going to end up playing video games one way or another, then laying that foundation becomes extremely important so that you can fall back. Otherwise, they’re stepping into something that they’ve had no experience in. So like anything else as a parent, it’s a little bit of a responsibility to know how you’re going to lay that foundation to allow for a healthy growth as they get older.”

	Games for Change initiative Raising Good Gamers launched a pilot parent workshop earlier this year for parents that asked families to build their own code of conduct for gaming, setting shared expectations that their children helped shape. By the end of the workshop, 82% of participants felt more confident talking with their children about gaming. 

	This September, the parenting workshop will be offered more widely through in-person events at community organizations across the U.S. and U.K., as well as through online webinars, with Kowert’s SPACE framework included.
	

	“We are trying to encourage curious parenting,” Shapiro says. “So it’s very obvious there’s no way that we’re going to lead a successful workshop or have a successful interaction with parents if we’re just giving a laundry list of the games that are out there and what they should look for and what is good and what is bad because that’s ever changing. What we’re trying to do is create a method for helping parents understand how they can have the conversations with their children to understand what their kids are playing, what they like about it, why they want to play.”

schema.headline: Why Parents Are Still Afraid of Video Games After 50 Years and How a Gaming Nonprofit’s New Workshops Are Trying to Help

title: Kevin Feige on ‘Brand New Day’ Breaking Records, Sadie Sink’s Reveal and Tom Holland Getting a ‘Restful Victory Lap’ Before a Potential ‘Spider-Man 5’
description: Kevin Feige can’t stop breaking his own box office benchmarks. As the president of Marvel Studios and architect of the sprawling, ultra-successful M
body:
Kevin Feige can’t stop breaking his own box office benchmarks. As the president of Marvel Studios and architect of the sprawling, ultra-successful Marvel Cinematic Universe, Feige is now responsible for the four biggest opening weekends in history.

	His latest record-setting blockbuster is “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which collected a dizzying $360 million in its domestic debut and supplanted 2019’s “Avengers: Endgame” ($357 million) as the biggest opening weekend ever. To get a sense of the size and scale of the accomplishment, the third- and fourth-largest launches — 2021’s “Spider-Man: No Way Home” with $260 million and 2018’s “Avengers: Infinity War” with $257 million — earned $100 million less to start and still became two of the highest-grossing movies of all time. All that’s to say, there’s no telling where “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” the 38th installment in the MCU, will wind up by the end of its theatrical run. With $932 million globally after three (!) days in theaters, the Tom Holland-led superhero adventure will cross $1 billion at a near-record clip and should climb to $2 billion in no time.
	

	“It’s overwhelming, frankly, to find ourselves in this position on a Monday morning,” says Feige. “In the very best way.”


	“Brand New Day,” Holland’s fourth solo outing as Spider-Man, follows the aftermath of the titular web-slinger’s pivotal decision in “No Way Home” to erase his identity from the world in order to salvage the multiverse. He’s still fighting crime, but Marvel’s friendly, neighborhood hero is seriously struggling without his pals (Zendaya and Jacob Batalon) by his side, and with a mysterious entity (Sadie Sink has something to do with that) threatening New York City.
	

	After a historic weekend at the box office, Feige spoke to Variety about Tom Holland’s enduring popularity as Peter Parker, Sink’s grand MCU debut, and what the success of “Brand New Day” means for December’s epic crossover event, “Avengers: Doomsday.”
	
		Prior to this weekend, did you ever think another movie could open to more than $300 million? After all, “Avengers: Endgame” — the only other movie to achieve those initial heights — was the culmination of 22 interconnected films.	

	I didn’t — for all the reasons I don’t think anyone did, because of COVID, because of the beating that theatrical took for so long. But once the bar had been raised, it could be raised again, right? The first movie to ever cross $100 million over opening weekend was Sam Raimi’s “Spider-Man.” The first to cross $150 million in one weekend was Sam Raimi’s “Spider-Man 3.” The first to $200 million was the first “Avengers.” And then, of course, the first to $300 million was “Endgame.” We did think that things could increase, but the past five or six years didn’t necessarily feel like that was the case. That’s a long-winded way of saying I did not expect “Endgame’s” record to be beat, but I couldn’t be happier that it was beat this past weekend by our 38th MCU movie.
	
		The debuts of “Brand New Day” and “Endgame” are $100 million above the next-biggest opening weekends. How did this movie rise to that level of popularity?	

	It’s a testament to [director] Destin Daniel Cretton, Tom Holland, and [producer] Amy Pascal. And [Sony Pictures chairman] Tom Rothman, for letting us do this four times now — working to bring Spidey to the screen. It’s a testament to what Stan Lee and Steve Ditko created all those years ago. People can write about changing tastes, but as characters that grow and evolve through the decades, there are none better than the Marvel characters — and none better than Peter Parker. When you find an actor like Tom Holland to bring that character to life, it is the magic formula.
	
		It’s hard to imagine Tom Holland ever departing the role. Are there plans to make another “Spider-Man” movie with him?	

	There are always plans. But right now, he’s going to rest after that global tour. He and Zendaya are going to take a good and restful victory lap, which they very much deserve.
	
	
		Why did you want to keep Sadie Sink’s casting a secret?	

	It’s purely about creating the best possible opening weekend experience for the audience. Sadie’s character is one that our fans know has immense significance within the Marvel Universe, and she plays a key role in the future of the MCU. I’m just happy that the secret is finally out and that Sadie can stop dodging the question.
	
		How does “Brand New Day” set up the MCU moving forward?	

	For people who’ve seen “Brand New Day,” they know the storyline leads us into more “Spider-Man” films and into the future of the MCU. And, I think we’re still in spoiler territory because the movie only just came out, but it leads into another very well-known Marvel franchise created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby.
	
		There was a time when superhero movies couldn’t miss at the box office. What have you learned from recent hits and misses in the genre?	

	I can only speak to “Brand New Day,” and audiences responded to a movie that’s well-crafted and well-made. They don’t always do that. But when they do, it’s a nice reminder that success builds success. “The Odyssey,” “Toy Story 5” and all the great movies that have been in theaters this year reminds people there’s nothing like a shared experience. There’s nothing like a moment for the whole globe to come together. 
	
		With some of the recent misses, though, it feels like audiences are getting tired of more of the same story. Do you agree?	

	Many things can be true at once. I think last year’s “Fantastic Four” looked and sounded like nothing that had been done in a superhero movie before, and it only [grossed] $521 million. “Brand New Day” is very directly a part four. It picks up right after the events of “Spider-Man: No Way Home,” and yet it tells a story that resonates. It’s ultimately about loneliness and the dangers of staying in our apartments by ourselves, looking at our phones. That resonates across cultures and across the globe right now.
	
		What does the excitement for “Brand New Day” mean for “Doomsday” in December?	

	For “Avengers: Doomsday” and “X Men,” it bodes very well. When a shared universe works, these are the results.

schema.headline: Kevin Feige on ‘Brand New Day’ Breaking Records, Sadie Sink’s Reveal and Tom Holland Getting a ‘Restful Victory Lap’ Before a Potential ‘Spider-Man 5’

title: Costume Designer Arianne Phillips on How Madonna Inspired ‘I Want Your Sex,’ and Finding Olivia Wilde’s Frustrated Artist Look for ‘The Invite’
description: Olivia Wilde once called costume designer Arianne Phillips “one of the greatest costume designers in film history.” Phillips worked with Wilde on “D
body:
Olivia Wilde once called costume designer Arianne Phillips “one of the greatest costume designers in film history.” Phillips worked with Wilde on “Don’t Worry Darling,” and when it came to “The Invite,” the pair reunited again.

	When she got the call, Phillips immediately said yes to the film, which Wilde both directed and starred in. Phillips says of her collaborator, “Olivia has such a consistency in her vision; she’s such a great director to work with. She’s a bit of a unicorn because she has a very distinctive vision and point of view, yet she makes space to graciously take in everyone’s ideas.”
	

	Their partnership didn’t end there. Wilde and Phillips also worked together on Gregg Araki’s “I Want Your Sex.” In that film, Wilde stars as Erika Tracy, a sexually charged artist who turns her charm on Cooper Hoffman’s Elliot, a 23-year-old college grad who quickly succumbs to her sexual advances and lavish fantasies. Phillips says, “I would say this about Olivia: she is fearless. She’s brave as a director, but she’s equally very brave as an actor. She’s not self-conscious at all about her body.” Phillips adds, “I learned so much as someone who’s always been overly self-conscious. She’s really willing to try anything. There’s nothing she’s not willing to try.”


	Here Phillips breaks down some of the key looks from both films and her experience working with Wilde.

	‘The Invite’



	

	



	As Phillips read the script by Will McCormick and Rashida Jones, it struck her how much it read like a play. “It’s such an ensemble piece; in terms of the rhythm of the story, it’s like opening an oyster,” she says.
	

	The film is set over the course of one evening, which sharply limited the number of looks for the cast. Wilde stars as Angela, married to Joe, played by Seth Rogen. The pair are a married couple whose relationship is on thin ice. When they invite their “loud” upstairs neighbors, Pina (Penélope Cruz) and Hawk (Edward Norton), for an intimate dinner party, things take an unexpected turn.

	Phillips faced a challenge: reducing down who the characters were. “I could help give story clues, and at the same time find costumes that would evolve over the course of the film,” she explains. “With Hawk and Pina, I didn’t want to set them up with any preconceptions. I wanted the audience to discover who they are in real time through the dialogue and the acting.”

	In early meetings with Wilde, the film’s production designer Jade Healy and the film’s cinematographer Adam Newport-Berra, Phillips understood how the doorways and windows created what she calls “beautiful framing.” She says, “I thought of the costumes like portraits or photographs and said, ‘What if we took portraits of them? What would we learn about them?’”

	Angela and Joe



	

	



	Crafting Angela’s look was a collaborative process with Wilde. Angela is a stay-at-home mom with artistic sensibility, Phillips says. “She’s a frustrated artist. She’s expressing herself through the way she decorates the home. We learn she found that rug at the flea market.” It later becomes a talking point between the couples and almost a point of contention for her husband, Joe.

	But Angela had style, which Phillips describes as “really reminiscent of Diane Keaton, who was a goalpost for us.” She continues, “When I think of Diane Keaton, I think of this incredible eclectic personal style; I wanted Angela to emit that.” She continues, “The idea that she has a ‘40s blouse … she’s effortlessly stylish wearing overalls.”

	Angela wears vintage cowboy boots with embroidery and a striped T-shirt with a 1940s jacket.

	As for her main outfit, the original idea was to put her in pants so Wilde could have freedom to move. Then the idea of a mint green dress also came up, but the final outfit ended up being a mint green blouse. “It’s eclectic. I tried to express a lot through jewelry and accessories to give her a layer of personality. “She has mismatched earrings, and a 1970s Hermes Medor watch that was from my personal collection.” Phillips notes, “She’s nervous about the neighbors coming over. Olivia really loved the idea that her creative identity is so absorbed into the apartment that she blends into the walls.” She adds, ”Her blouse is buttoned up, so there’s a sense of presentation and appropriateness.”
	

	Phillips says when it came to Joe, she wanted him to look like he just didn’t care. “Maybe Angela bought his clothes?” His style was more about comfort. She explains, “He is a semi-depressed guy who’s not fulfilled in his daily life.”

	With Joe and Angela in near-matching color palettes, Phillips admits, “That was really challenging for me. I was fighting my own aesthetic. Normally, I would never put them both in blue-green tones next to each other because it clashed.” Phillips admits she felt tempted to change Rogen’s shirt, but after camera tests, she changed her mind. “I like the fact that they’re in a similar light palette, but it’s off and clashing because that shows the disconnect they’re having in their relationship. There’s no real color harmony.”

	Pina and Hawk



	

	



	As a sexologist, Phillips loosely based Pina on Esther Perel. “I didn’t want her to look like a textbook psychiatrist. We wanted her to have a sense of sexuality, and so that was really about silhouette.” The more audiences learn about Pina and her story, the more she takes her layers off. “She’s undressing more.”

	Phillips noted how Cruz was expressive with her hands. Knowing how Wilde and Newport-Berra were going to shoot the film in a very intimate way, Phillips says, “I started with the idea of wanting her to have rings because rings were an opportunity to highlight her hands and catch light with the camera.” Phillips used rings from local L.A. designer Hillary Heydle. One ring that stood out was a pearl design. “Pearls are sexual for obvious reasons. Hillary also had a gold goddess ring with an imprint of a Botticelli-esque goddess. Pina also wore a lovely, sexy ear cuff from a designer I discovered online from Barcelona.”

	Hawk had a masculine simplicity. Phillips says, “I like this idea of this macho guy wearing dark, subtle colors. It’s about his physique as an ex-fireman, and he takes his pants off, and he’s wearing like bright red underwear.” Phillips adds, “The only flourish I gave him was a beaded man bracelet, designed by Joseph Brooks, and his work has a bird logo tag. I thought the idea of hawk, bird, freedom worked.” She continues, “I believe that it is important to create costumes that help move the story and express who the characters are. So, even if there’s little things that the audience doesn’t see, they have it.
	

	Costume Designer title card

	In the film’s opening credits, Phillips is given a title card that comes early as opposed to much later.

	When Phillips went to a cast and crew screening, she recalls almost falling out of her seat after seeing her name come up. She explains, “Traditionally, a costume designer comes after the editor and/or it’s around the music credit.” After the film, she approached the film’s producer Saul Germaine, who said, “That was on purpose. Olivia made sure of that, and I was just gobsmacked.’”

	‘I Want Your Sex’

	For Araki’s movie, Phillips went from a single costume with Wilde to an explosion of costumes.

	T-shirt nods



	

									Courtesy Arianne Phillips Instagram
	



	In one scene, Elliot is wearing a vintage Madonna Rebel Heart Tour T-shirt. He wears it in bed as he masturbates. Phillips worked with Madonna for over 20 years, collaborating on tours, photo shoots, and music videos, as well as designing the costumes for Madonna’s “W.E.”

	“Cooper’s character wears a lot of T-shirts, and for the masturbation scene, I thought, ‘We definitely have to have a good T-shirt there, and my first inclination was it should be Madonna.” Phillips continues, “She would think it’s hilarious. We had to have all kinds of paperwork and agreements, letting them know. I love that T-shirt because her name’s at the top. So yes, and Madonna approved it.”

	Other T-shirts Phillips used were nods to Quentin Tarantino’s “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Phillips was the film’s costume designer and put Apple (Chase Sui Wonders) in a Spahn Ranch T-shirt.

	Erika’s Madonna-Inspired Look



	

									Lacey Terrell
	



	Knowing Araki’s body of work, Phillips knew the filmmaker liked color and wanted a sense of hyperrealism. “That was initially a challenge for Phillips because the colors associated with BDSM are typically black and metallic.”

	Wilde and Phillips collaborated to discover Erika. “Olivia and I talked a lot about early Madonna, ‘Human Nature, the BDSM erotica, the ‘Sex’ book, and that whole Madonna era, which is right before I started working with her. In my 23 years of working with Madonna, we were touching on different BDSM looks, so I had a lot of resources.”

	Phillips also rewatched “Eating Raoul” with Mary Woronov who plays a dominatrix housewife. Dita Von Teese’s burlesque act also served as another inspiration. “Olivia looks great in everything. So in a way, it’s always editing and editing and figuring out the tone.”
	



	

	



	Co-designing with Monica Chamberlain

	Phillips co-designed the film with costume designer Monica Chamberlain. She explains there was no prep time, no real budget and so many costumes. Phillips admits, “I knew I couldn’t do it alone, and the crew is small. Monica Chamberlain had been my assistant designer on a few films, and she wanted to co-design, and it’s important with people who you have relationships with who work on your crew to help them move up.” She adds, “It was really great generationally to co-design with someone younger than me.

	“I took the lead with Erica, and she took the lead with Elliot, and then we cross-pollinated with everyone else, and it was just a great experience.”

	Erika’s burgundy look was by Vex Clothing. Phillips explains, “You can’t get anything that’s more second skin or and has a sexuality to it, so we had to have some latex pieces. At this point, it’s almost redundant to have latex, but I thought that color was really good. It was an off color. It’s not every day you see a burgundy latex.”

	Madonna

	Having worked with Madonna for over two decades, Phillips says, “Madonna broke so many boundaries with what she was doing with the ‘Erotica’ album and her ‘Sex’ book, that it became part of the lexicon in a way. Before that, it was relegated to like porn, or you know, she kind of made it fashion.”

Olivia Wilde says it was "liberating" playing a dominatrix in Gregg Araki's "I Want Your Sex": "It was the least amount of clothing I've ever worn on a set." pic.twitter.com/JcyCzxXbxP— Variety (@Variety) July 29, 2026

title: Every ‘Spider-Man’ Movie Ranked From Worst to Best
description:
Aug 3, 2026 11:50am PT	
	

			


			
			
	

									Everett Collection
	

		
	
				
Throughout two decades of web-slinging, rebootin
body:
Aug 3, 2026 11:50am PT	
	

			


			
			
	

									Everett Collection
	

		
	
				
Throughout two decades of web-slinging, rebooting, reversals of fortune, immersions into the Marvel Cinematic Universe and sporadic reappearances by the Spidey-hating J. Jonah Jameson, the “Spider-Man” film franchise has been wildly inconsistent, yet remarkably indestructible.
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” the latest film, broke box office records this weekend after it swung its way to a mind-blowing $360 million domestic opening. It’s the biggest box office launch of all time, after setting records for the largest preview haul and opening day, and beat “Avengers: Endgame” for the historic honor. Tom Holland has now starred in the four highest box office openings of all time: “Brand New Day,” “Endgame,” “Avengers: Infinity War” and “Spider-Man: No Way Home.” After several superhero movies have misfired at the box office, it’s clear there’s no such thing as Spider-Man fatigue.
Spidey has been swinging to box office heights across live-action and animation. “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse,” the previous entry, was a follow-up to the Oscar-winning animated feature “Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse” (2018). It delighted many long-time fans with its mythos-expanding plotting, quicksilver universe shuffling, abundant Easter Eggs, wide-ranging inclusivity, and audaciously variegated visuals — even if it totally confused, if not actively annoyed, newbies unfamiliar with the minutiae of what someone here aptly refers to as “the canon.” “Beyond the Spider-Verse” will put a bow on the animated trilogy when it releases on June 18, 2027.
Naturally, the Spider Dude also continues to attract legions of the faithful to animated TV series and direct-to-video product, all-star MCU group gatherings — and, yes, the comic books that started it all. But the 11 theatrical features — movies in which Spider-Man is the star, not an ensemble player — are our focus here in this revised least-to-best ranking.   


			
			
	The Amazing Spider-Man 2 (2014)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Eve				
					
				The longest (until “Spider-Man: No Way Home”) and least of the Spidey movies is a ponderously overstuffed misfire only partially redeemed by the chemistry generated between Andrew Garfield and Emma Stone. Having learned nothing from the debacle of “Batman and Robin” (1997), the filmmakers cram no fewer than three classic comic book villains — Electro, a reimagined Green Goblin and, fleetingly, Rhino — into a padded narrative, demonstrating once again that, yes, more can be less. Originally intended as the gateway to an extended universe of Spidey sagas, complete with Sinister Six spin-offs, “Amazing 2” instead led to a second franchise reboot. — Joe Leydon
		
			
			
	Spider-Man 3 (2007)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Sony Pictures/Courtesy Everett				
					
				If you watch all three of director Sam Raimi’s Spidey movies back-to-back, it’s impressive to see how smoothly each flows into the next. Alas, the flow was stemmed fairly early in this disappointing threequel, as Tobey Maguire’s moody web-slinger wobbled between smug swagger and vengeful wrath while battling an indifferently conceived supervillain (Thomas Haden Church’s underwhelming Sandman) and his own Venom-fueled dark side. Even some diehard Spider-fans couldn’t help guffawing while the “Bad” Peter Parker tried to strut and smooth-move like someone suffering from “Saturday Night Fever.” Others could only wonder: Does being bitten by a radioactive spider really turn you into a grandstanding jazz pianist? — Joe Leydon
		
			
			
	The Amazing Spider-Man (2012)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Eve				
					
				Fairly or not, Andrew Garfield likely will be recalled as the George Lazenby of the Spider-Man movies, given his relatively short stint as the second star of the franchise. (Spoiler Alert: He eventually gets some big laughs with a few wink-wink, nudge-nudge allusions to his status in the Spidey-Verse.) But give him due credit: Garfield strikes the right balance of callowness and cockiness throughout the “origin story” of this reboot, and he’s downright charming as director Marc Webb (“500 Days of Summer”) dramatizes the first blush of romance between nerdy Peter Parker and Emma Stone’s equally brainy but intimidatingly attractive Gwen Stacy. (A nice touch: Gwen is the slightly better science student.) On the debit side: The conspiratorial subplot involving Peter’s deceased scientist father is a great deal less than fully baked, and the villain of the piece (The Lizard, played by Rhys Ifans while in human form) is too obviously a CGI construct. — Joe Leydon
		
			
			
	Spider-Man: Far From Home (2019)
			
										
					Image Credit: Jay Maidment/Sony Pictures				
					
				
In a post-“Avengers: Endgame” world, Peter Parker must press on without the mentorship of a now-deceased Tony Stark — but with the high-tech resources of Stark Enterprises (represented by Jon Favreau’s Happy Hogan) and the gruff encouragement of S.H.I.E.L.D. honcho Nick Fury (Samuel L. Jackson). Unfortunately, while there is ample excitement to be savored during this follow-up to “Spider-Man: Homecoming,” a dandy villain in Jake Gyllenhaal’s
Mysterio, and with some charming give-and-take between Tom Holland’s Spidey/Parker and Zendaya’s MJ Jones, the movie continues the MCU trend of steadily transforming Spider-Man from a solo super hero who relies on his own grit and brains to defeat bad guys to an under-achieving team player who must don an Iron-Manly outfit before he can fight the good fight. For all its considerable merits, this may be the first Spider-Man film that will appeal more to relative newbies than long-time fans of the original Marvel Comics. On the other hand, it’s amusing to see at the end that J. Jonah Jameson (J.K. Simmons), merely an anti-Spidey newspaper editor in earlier films, has been effectively reconstituted as a ranting-and-raving multimedia Spidey hater. — Joe Leydon
		
			
			
	Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse (2023)
			
										
					Image Credit: Sony Pictures Animation				
					
				
	Call it too much of a good thing and you won’t be far off the mark. The second animated “Spider-Man” feature focuses on neophyte Spidey Miles Morales, slightly older and marginally wiser than he was in “Into the Spider-Verse,” but also gives near-equal time to his sweetie, the equally arachnid-enhanced Gwen Stacy, a.k.a. Spider-Woman — and adds to the mix a veritable army of distinctive Spider-People, who each do derring-do in their individual corners of the multiverse when they’re not banded together in a Spider Society designed to maintain borders and discourage interlopers. Trouble is, the start-and-stop pacing required to accommodate so many new folks makes for a bumpy ride, as turbo-charged action sequences that often recall the framing and flamboyance of the original comics are interspersed with buzz-killing stretches of backstory spinning and meandering character development. Worse, this sporadically impressive but discomfortingly overstuffed extravaganza concludes with a brazenly shameless “To Be Continued” cliffhanger that could very well inspire members of the audience to shout rude things at the screen. — Joe Leydon
		
			
			
	Spider-Man: Brand New Day (2026)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Tom Holland’s Spidey gets dark — real dark — in “Brand New Day,” which picks up after the world forgets Peter Parker’s identity at the end of “No Way Home.” That leaves the hero all alone without the support of MJ, his best pal Ned (Jacob Batalon), the Avengers or his late Aunt May. A standout Sadie Sink plays the film’s villain (her identity is a major spoil but bodes well for the future of the MCU), whose body-possessing powers are as unsettling as they are unique to what we’ve seen in the superhero universe thus far. Sink is far from the only evildoer in the movie; there’s also some comic-book deep cuts like Scorpion (Michael Mando), Tombstone (Marvin Jones III), Ramrod, Boomerang, Tarantula and the Hand ninja cabal. The eclectic cast of characters, including Mark Ruffalo’s Hulk and Jon Bernthal’s Punisher, make the movie feel like a living, breathing comic that’s part of an interconnected world. Holland gives one of his best performances as Peter and Spider-Man as he undergoes a stress-induced transformation that puts his powers on the fritz. Destin Daniel Cretton, who helmed Marvel’s martial arts action-inspired “Shang-Chi,” deftly takes the wheel on “Brand New Day,” giving us a fresh take on Holland’s hero from what we’ve seen in this three standalone and two team-up appearances. — Jordan Moreau
		
			
			
	Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (2018)
			
										
					Image Credit: Sony Pictures Animation				
					
				Winner of the Academy Award for Animated Feature, this dramatically and visually exhilarating Spidey adventure is at once respectfully faithful to its comic-book roots — with a wink-wink here and there, of course — and exuberantly  free-wheeling in its incorporation of other pop-culture influences both multifaceted and multicultural. The underlying conceit: Each parallel universe gets the Spider-Man it deserves and needs. (Obviously, radioactive spiders are a constant everywhere.) So when there is a passing of the mask from veteran web-slinger Peter Parker to eager novice Miles Morales in our world, he’s able to draw on the assistance of such other-worldly Spideys as a hardboiled Spider-Man Noir (voiced by Nicolas Cage) and an out-of-shape but game-for-action Peter B. Parker (Jake Johnson). It is meant as high praise to say the screenplay credited to Phil Lord and Rodney Rothman would have worked just as well in a live-action film. — Joe Leydon
		
			
			
	Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Disney				
					
				The creative folks behind the second franchise reboot score points for eschewing a conventional “origin story” — obviously, they figured everyone who buys a ticket to a Spider-Man movie already knows how the dude got his super powers. (And those who didn’t surely were brought up to speed when Spidey cameoed in 2016’s “Captain America: Civil War.”) Better still, they audaciously jumpstart the running-on-fumes movie mythos by re-imagining the man behind the mask as a boy — specifically, an eager-but-awkward 15-year-old Peter Parker (Tom Holland) who has a lot to learn from Tony Stark/Iron Man (Robert Downey Jr.) when it comes to doing derring-do. But wait, there’s more: Michael Keaton earns a place of honor in the pantheon of Spidey villains by effectively playing The Vulture as a fortuitously empowered blue-collar type raging with class resentment directed at one-percenters like, well, Tony Stark. — Joe Leydon
		
			
			
	Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Sony Pictures				
					
				It’s practically impossible without spilling scads of spoilers to fully explain why this third Spidey film featuring Tom Holland as the resourceful teen webslinger is so excitingly entertaining, emotionally affecting and abundantly satisfying for both relative newcomers to the Marvel Cinematic Universe — including those who know relatively little about the friendly neighborhood hero prior to 2002’s “Spider-Man” — and those of us who have been Spidey fans as far back the first issue of “The Amazing Spider-Man,” wherein a cash-poor Spidey broke into the Baxter Building in the hope of auditioning for a high-paying gig with the Fantastic Four. (No, I’m not making that up.) Suffice it to say that director John Watts and scripters Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers cleverly sample and scramble many elements — along with heroes and villains — from earlier episodes in the franchise while constructing the cinematic equivalent of a legendary entertainer’s “Greatest Hits” LP, an inspired mashup strategy that stands in marked contrast to the maladroit inclusivity of “The Amazing Spider-Man 2.” (A nice touch: J.K. Simmons’ Spidey-hating J. Jonah Jameson lives down to expectations by going full Alex Jones here.) But wait, there’s more: They also ingeniously bring the character — and the franchise — back to Ground Zero, evoking a time when Spidey couldn’t rely on support from mentors like Iron Man or Dr. Strange, and even had to sew his own Spidey suit. — Joe Leydon
		
			
			
	Spider-Man 2 (2004)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Eve				
					
				Director Sam Raimi and Original Gangsta Spidey Tobey Maguire made lightning strike a second time in their first sequel to the groundbreaking 2002 franchise kickoff. Although it may be difficult to appreciate now, after the massive expansion of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, this film’s canny mix of super-heroics, human drama and (by then-contemporary standards) cutting-edge special effects still had novelty value going for it when “Spider-Man 2” first hit theaters. And the passing of time has done nothing to diminish the entertainment value of Maguire’s engaging portrait of the superhero as a fallible young man. (Even more fallible here after a temporary, psychosomatic power loss.) Co-star Kirsten Dunst (Mary Jane Watson), James Franco (Harry Osborn), and Rosemary Harris (Aunt May), along with comic-reliever J.K. Simmons (J. Jonah Jameson), remind us just how perfectly cast they were in the previous movie. And Alfred Molina triumphantly upstages the CGI trickery employed to enhance his character as the demented Dr. Octopus, arguably the greatest villain in the entire Spidey franchise. — Joe Leydon
		
			
			
	Spider-Man (2002)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Eve				
					
				Much like a first kiss (or, in this case, an upside-down smooch) always seems the sweetest, the first “Spider-Man” movie remains the most purely enjoyable movie in the franchise. Indeed, there’s something not entirely unlike an air of innocence wafting about the entire enterprise as Tobey Maguire miraculously obtains, initially misuses, and ultimately focuses his superpowers, all the while pining for (and, briefly, winning) the seemingly impossible object of his desire, Kirsten Dunst’s girl-next-door Mary Jane Watson. A few diehard Marvel Comics fans quibbled about some evocations of artistic license — in the world according to director Sam Raimi and scripter David Koepp, Spidey’s web is natural fiber, not synthetic additive — but “Spider-Man” as a whole proved largely faithful to its source material, particularly in its repeated questioning of whether the hero might ever catch a break. And that contributed generously to its huge success. Pay no heed to the nitpickers who might complain that the once-awesome special effects now appear a tad dated. The only thing still worth debating is: Did Willem Dafoe actually intend to sound so much like Gilbert Gottfried while playing the villainous Green Goblin? — Joe Leydon
		
	
	


	
		More from Variety

In-N-Out Mass Shooting

                            11:57 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The In-N-Out employee who died when a gunman shot up her workplace over the weekend in Idaho has been identified ... and her friends and family are reeling.
      
    
            Ashley Garibay, a 23-year-old from Stockton, California, was among the 3 killed and 7 injured when Chad Williams opened fire with an assault-style rifle -- before he killed himself ... according to the Daily Mail.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Ashley's family and friends flooded Facebook with messages of heartbreak and shock, with one person saying, "Ashley you are so beautiful. You will be missed so much."
      

            In-N-Out President Lynsi Snyder said the employee who died was working the drive-thru when she was shot, adding ... "My heart is broken, my chest is heavy, my eyes burn from the tears I've shed."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As we previously reported ... the mayhem began Saturday afternoon at the burger joint in Twin Falls -- a city in southern Idaho -- where the gunman opened fire before an armed civilian and off-duty officer shot back.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            A motive for the gunman is still unknown.
      
    
            Ashley was only 23.
      
    
            RIP

body:
Sid Wilson's Slipknot Firing
                          Band Mates Were Fed Up With Him!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 3, 2026
                            11:14 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 3, 2026
                                1:41 PM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sid Wilson's exit from Slipknot may have stunned fans ... but his bandmates had been ready to pull the plug for quite some time ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Sources with direct knowledge tell TMZ ... the decision came after the group finally had enough of Sid's behavior ... namely, the way he treated his bandmates.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told the firing was a long time coming -- not some abrupt decision made in the heat of the moment.
      

            In fact, our sources say Slipknot was planning to announce Sid's departure this week ... but the band lost control of the rollout when we first reported Friday the group's longtime DJ and keyboardist had been permanently kicked out.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told the early reveal caused the band to freak out behind the scenes ... with members frustrated they could no longer announce the split on their own terms.
      
    
            We broke the story ... Sid was informed Friday afternoon that he was officially out after more than 25 years with the heavy metal group.
      
    
            He joined Slipknot in 1999 and was one of its nine original members.
      
    
            The firing comes on the heels of his split from Kelly Osbourne back in March.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            They quietly called off their engagement ... but our sources have said there's still a chance they could get back together.
      
    
            Sid resurfaced Sunday outside a Los Angeles recording studio ... but he kept his head down and stayed silent when asked point-blank about the firing.
      
    
            Slipknot hasn't publicly addressed Sid's departure ... but behind the masks, we're told the breakup had been brewing for a long time.

body:
Ariana Grande's Mom
                          Shows Pop Star Support ...
                          Amid Personal Struggles
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 3, 2026
                            1:15 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Ariana Grande's mom is showing support for the singer amid her team announcing she will be stepping out of the spotlight following her "Eternal Sunshine" tour due to public criticism.
      
    
            Ariana's beloved mom Joan took to the comment section on her latest Instagram post, saying, "You are magnificent... and this video is incredible!!"
      
    
            Joan continues with, "I love it and I love you more!!!"
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The support comes amid Ariana's rep announcing she will be distancing herself from public view due to recent online opinions ... blaming the "endless, ongoing public scrutiny" surrounding her public appearances.
      
    
            Fans have recently voiced concern over Ariana's noticeably slimmer appearance, with many pointing to her latest music video for "Petal" -- the same video Joan was praising in her encouraging message, making her comments an especially timely show of support as online speculation surrounding Ariana continues.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Ariana's fans weren't the only ones to lay down their opinion on her appearance, as 'Good Place' actress Jameela Jamil sounded the alarm Saturday over Ariana's appearance ... claiming the pop star is "possibly dying right in front of us."
      
    
            The "hate that I made you love me" singer has not responded to Jameela's claims ... a source close to the singer told PEOPLE she performs her highly physical show "healthily and successfully at a very high level night after night."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Ariana has repeatedly pushed back against commentary about her body over the years ... reminding fans in 2023 that the appearance people once considered her "healthiest" actually came during an unhealthy period in her life.

body:
Dr. Dre
                          Same Restaurant, New Nobu Boo!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 3, 2026
                            12:50 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Dr. Dre is back for date night at Nobu Malibu ... but this time, he's not dining with "The Valley" star Michelle Saniei ... he's breaking bread with a different brunette.
      
    
            The music mogul was photographed walking closely beside the a mystery woman as they exited the restaurant Sunday ... unclear who she is, but she's not the reality TV star who only recently confirmed she was dating Dre.
      
    
            His dinner companion dressed up for the evening in a pastel mini dress and carried what appeared to be a matching Hermes Mini Kelly bag. Dre kept things casual in all black.
      

            It's unclear whether the pair were on a date or simply grabbing dinner as friends, but the location makes the outing especially interesting.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Dre and Michelle had previously been photographed holding hands after dinner at Nobu Malibu, helping spark romance rumors she later confirmed.
      
    
            Michelle eventually said she and Dre were spending time together and loved being in each other's company. She also revealed they were introduced through a mutual friend, though she said they intended to keep the relationship largely private.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported, Michelle's ex-husband, Jesse Lally, said he learned about the relationship online and was not given a heads-up. Most of Michelle's Bravo castmates were also initially in the dark.
      
    
            No word if Michelle was in the dark about Dre's new Malibu dinner guest ... but she's about to find out!!!
